title: vSphere Resource Pool Hard-Limit Inventory
exclusions: Returns resource-pool configuration snapshots with a finite CPU or memory limit. Broadcom defines `ResourceAllocationInfo.limit` as maximum allowed usage, in MHz for CPU and MB for memory, and `-1` as no fixed limit; a finite limit is valid configuration and is not inherently misconfiguration, contention, throttling, high utilization, capacity shortage or impact. This inventory-only rule does not calculate utilization-to-limit percentage, reservations consumed, expandable-reservation borrowing, shares under contention, descendant scaling, admission control, DRS behavior or VM performance. The source/index/sourcetype and flattened pool fields are an explicit local scripted-input contract because Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics does not document a dedicated resource-pool configuration sourcetype. Missing snapshots and API failures are source-health findings. The rule changes no pool and makes no compliance claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain governed vCenter/resource-pool hierarchy and owners; read-only API account/privileges; scripted-input code, dependency lock, checkpoint, schedule, HEC/input and field contract; representative raw API responses with entity, CPU/memory allocation, shares, expandable reservation, changeVersion, lastModified and collection time; independent expected-pool/API/input/schema/freshness health; approved pool policy and changes; version-controlled `vsphere_resource_pool_hard_limits` SPL, ACL, schedule, dispatches and rows; dashboard/runbook and dispositions; and dated unlimited, CPU-only, memory-only, both-limited, zero-limit, blank, duplicate, delayed, moved/renamed and API-failure tests. This documentation review created no API collector, snapshot, search execution, resource change, alert or production validation evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In isolated local-contract fixtures, ingest pool `rp-prod` with CPU limit 12000 MHz and memory limit -1 MB, then pool `rp-batch` with CPU -1 and memory 32768 MB; include stable pool MOID, vCenter, names, reservations, shares and fresh collection time. Expect exactly two rows showing finite dimensions and UC-2.1.20. Repeat with both finite.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Expect zero inventory rows when both limits are exactly -1. Do not return rows for blank/invalid pool identity, vCenter, CPU/memory limits, wrong local source/sourcetype/index, stale/out-of-window records or exact duplicate snapshot. Separate health must surface missing expected pools, duplicate identities, unknown units/schema and API/input failures.

dataSources: Primary source is a governed local scripted input that uses the vSphere API to enumerate ResourcePool managed objects and retrieve each `ResourceConfigSpec`/`config`. Send one JSON snapshot per pool to a deployment-selected events index (example `index=vmware-config`), explicit local `source=vsphere_api:resourcepool_config` and explicit local `sourcetype=vmware:resourcepool:config`. Required normalized fields are vCenter, pool MOID/name/parent, `cpuAllocation.limit` and `.reservation` in MHz, `memoryAllocation.limit` and `.reservation` in MB, expandableReservation, shares, changeVersion, lastModified, collection time and API version. Splunk Add-on hierarchy inventory can corroborate pool name/parent but does not replace this local configuration contract.
app: A version-controlled local Splunk scripted/modular input or external collector uses a least-privilege vSphere API account and writes resource-pool config JSON through a governed input/HEC token. Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics (Splunkbase 5089) is optional for hierarchy, VM and performance corroboration. A local app owns the collector, field contract, health, search, dashboard, tests and runbook.
spl:
index=vmware-config source="vsphere_api:resourcepool_config" sourcetype="vmware:resourcepool:config" earliest=-2h@h latest=-1h@h
| eval vcenter=lower(trim(vcenter)), pool_moid=trim(pool_moid), pool_name=trim(pool_name), cpu_limit_mhz=tonumber('cpuAllocation.limit'), memory_limit_mb=tonumber('memoryAllocation.limit'), cpu_reservation_mhz=tonumber('cpuAllocation.reservation'), memory_reservation_mb=tonumber('memoryAllocation.reservation')
| where len(vcenter)>0 AND len(pool_moid)>0 AND len(pool_name)>0 AND isnotnull(cpu_limit_mhz) AND isnotnull(memory_limit_mb)
| stats latest(_time) AS snapshot_time latest(_indextime) AS snapshot_index_time latest(parent_moid) AS parent_moid latest(cpu_limit_mhz) AS cpu_limit_mhz latest(memory_limit_mb) AS memory_limit_mb latest(cpu_reservation_mhz) AS cpu_reservation_mhz latest(memory_reservation_mb) AS memory_reservation_mb latest(changeVersion) AS change_version latest(lastModified) AS config_last_modified BY vcenter pool_moid pool_name
| where cpu_limit_mhz!=-1 OR memory_limit_mb!=-1
| eval finite_cpu_limit=if(cpu_limit_mhz!=-1,"true","false"), finite_memory_limit=if(memory_limit_mb!=-1,"true","false"), use_case="UC-2.1.20"
| table snapshot_time vcenter pool_moid pool_name parent_moid cpu_limit_mhz memory_limit_mb cpu_reservation_mhz memory_reservation_mb finite_cpu_limit finite_memory_limit change_version config_last_modified snapshot_index_time use_case
| sort 0 vcenter pool_name
description: Lists the latest resource-pool configuration snapshot when CPU or memory has a finite hard limit, preserving CPU in MHz and memory in MB. Each row is configuration inventory for owner review, not evidence that the pool is currently constrained.
value: Hard limits can cap workloads even when parent capacity exists, but they can also implement deliberate service boundaries. A trustworthy inventory lets capacity owners reconcile each finite limit with policy, hierarchy and workload intent before incidents or changes, without pretending static configuration measures utilization.
implementation: Build a least-privilege vSphere API collector for ResourcePool config, define and test the local JSON source contract, and monitor expected-pool freshness separately. Run the delayed hourly latest-snapshot search, reconcile finite limits with policy/hierarchy/owners and performance, and require approved vSphere changes for any adjustment.
visualization: Use a hierarchy-aware table with vCenter, pool MOID/name/parent, CPU limit/reservation in MHz, memory limit/reservation in MB, finite flags, config revision/time, owner, policy, utilization corroboration and disposition. Add counts by parent/owner and separate expected-pool, API, schema and stale-snapshot panels. Never display a static limit as utilization percentage.
schema: Locally governed JSON projection of vSphere ResourcePool ResourceConfigSpec
dataModelAcceleration: No CIM dataset documents resource-pool allocation configuration and hierarchy. Keep the local raw JSON/API field contract authoritative; summary indexes may support trends only after parity checks.

references.title: Broadcom vSphere API: ResourceAllocationInfo units and -1 limit
Splunk: VMware Metrics inventory fields reference

knownFalsePositives:
A finite limit is not a false event; it is configuration requiring contextual review.

1. **Intentional service-tier boundary** — a pool may cap lower-priority workloads. Verify approved policy, owner, capacity analysis and review date.

2. **License or cost control** — limits can enforce contractual/resource boundaries. Confirm the exact requirement and impact assumptions.

3. **Temporary migration or test cap** — finite limits may support short experiments or transitions. Match change and finite expiry.

4. **Nested-pool design** — parent and descendant reservations/shares alter effective behavior. Review the complete hierarchy and expandable reservations.

5. **Idle pool** — a finite limit on an empty/unused pool is not current contention, but stale configuration still needs ownership.

6. **Collector/schema drift** — wrong numeric conversion, missing `-1`, API version or flattening change can create false finite flags. Compare raw API and contract tests.

7. **Duplicate/stale snapshot** — checkpoint replay or failed polling can preserve old configuration. Use MOID, changeVersion, lastModified and health.

8. **Rename/move** — names and parents can change while MOID remains the stable vCenter-scoped key. Reconcile hierarchy at snapshot time.

**Suppression mechanism:** use a governed post-result lookup keyed by vCenter and pool MOID plus exact changeVersion/limit pair, with policy, owner, reason and finite expiry/review date. Retain raw snapshots and expected-pool/API health; never suppress all finite limits under a parent.
mitreAttack: N/A (resource-allocation configuration inventory; no adversary behavior asserted)
hardware: vCenter ResourcePool managed objects and descendants. Effective workload behavior depends on hierarchy, shares, reservations, limits, contention and VM performance.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and local-contract boundary

Assign vSphere capacity, API, workload, Splunk and change owners. Inventory vCenters, ResourcePool MOIDs/hierarchy, policy, owners and expected polling. Broadcom defines CPU allocation in MHz, memory allocation in MB, reservation as guaranteed amount, and limit as maximum usage; `-1` means no fixed limit. A finite limit does not prove utilization or throttling.

Splunk Add-on for VMware Metrics documents hierarchy entities but no dedicated resource-pool config sourcetype/allocation-field contract. Therefore `index=vmware-config`, `source=vsphere_api:resourcepool_config` and `sourcetype=vmware:resourcepool:config` are explicit local conventions, not vendor add-on claims.

## Step 1 — Build and secure collection

Use the vSphere API ResourcePool config property through a version-pinned, reviewed collector. Enumerate stable pool managed-object references, retrieve ResourceConfigSpec, and emit one JSON event per pool with vCenter, pool MOID/name/parent, full cpuAllocation and memoryAllocation, changeVersion, lastModified, API version and collection time. Preserve raw response or a hash plus immutable collector revision.

Package the collector as a reviewed modular input or equivalent external service with a documented 60-minute poll interval. Use a least-privilege read-only vCenter account, TLS validation and secret storage. Send through a dedicated HEC token or scripted input with only target-index rights. Bound polling, pagination, retries and backoff; checkpoint by vCenter/pool without dropping unchanged-state heartbeats needed for freshness. Do not grant resource-pool update rights.

Validate raw API against vSphere Client Resource Pool > Configure > Resource Allocation for representative nested, unlimited and finite pools. Prove MHz/MB and `-1`. Build health for expected pools, API/HTTP status, auth, pagination, duplicate MOID, schema/type/unit, event count, stale/future time, checkpoint and HEC/index errors.

## Step 2 — Save the inventory search

Save sidecar SPL as `vsphere_resource_pool_hard_limits`, hourly. The delayed closed range allows one complete collection cycle; tune bounds to measured cadence without overlap.

The query fixes all local source identifiers, normalizes numeric allocation fields, requires pool identity and both limits, selects time-latest state by vCenter/MOID/name, and returns rows where either limit differs from -1. Zero is finite and can be highly restrictive; it must not be treated as unlimited. CPU and memory remain in native units. No utilization percentage is calculated.

## Step 3 — Validate semantics and hierarchy

Use fixtures for both unlimited, CPU-only, memory-only, both finite, zero, equal reservation/limit, reservation greater than malformed limit, blank, string/number type, duplicate snapshot, stale, rename/move, same MOID on different vCenters and API schema change. Assert units and exact `-1` behavior.

Compare current API, vSphere Client and Splunk at the same revision. Join separately to hierarchy and VM membership, then to resource-pool or descendant workload performance only after proving entity/time mapping. If utilization monitoring is desired, collect documented resource-pool performance counters with a separate tested contract; do not derive it from static allocation.

## Step 4 — Operationalize and respond

Dashboard limits/reservations with hierarchy, owner, policy, current corroborating demand and health. Triage by verifying raw snapshot/revision; checking current vSphere config; reviewing parent/descendant shares and expandable reservation; identifying affected VMs/service tiers; comparing performance/contention; and matching approved policy/change.

Never automatically set limit to -1, modify reservation/shares, move VMs or pools, or change DRS from inventory alone. Resource changes can shift contention or violate guarantees. Require capacity/workload approval, impact analysis, maintenance where needed, rollback and post-change evidence.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot

- Missing pool: verify API enumeration/pagination, permissions, deleted/moved object, checkpoint and expected inventory.
- `-1` parsed null: preserve signed numeric value and test JSON flattening/tonumber; never coerce missing to unlimited.
- Values disagree with UI: align vCenter, MOID, revision/time, parent context and units.
- Duplicate names: key on vCenter+MOID; names are display fields.
- No rows: verify at least one finite limit and source health; zero findings can be valid.
- Suspected throttling: collect resource-pool/VM demand, limit-hit and performance evidence; static config alone cannot prove impact.
- Collector fails: inspect API/TLS/auth/rate/pagination/HEC logs and alert through source health, not this inventory query.

Keep status draft until VMware, API and Splunk owners validate collector security, parity, fixtures and response. Documentation review does not instantiate or validate the local collector.
grandmaExplanation: We list virtual-machine resource groups that have a fixed ceiling on processor or memory use. A ceiling may be intentional, so the team checks the policy, the group hierarchy and real performance before changing it.
